questions.stem: The passage invites “Count diatonic triads / One per degree. / Counting the diatonic chords of a passage”. Which option is the evidence-backed one?

options.text: Four, including the leading tone triad
options.misconception: substitutes a familiar but inapplicable case for the relation the passage establishes

options.text: Three, only the primary triads
Seven, one on each scale degree
Twelve, one for each chromatic note

questions.explanation: Close reading of the note yields this rule: seven diatonic triads, one per scale degree. On that basis "Seven, one on each scale degree" is the supported choice. Option A ("Four, including the leading tone triad") fails because it substitutes a familiar but inapplicable case for counting the diatonic chords of a passage; Option B ("Three, only the primary triads") fails because it limits to primary triads; Option D ("Twelve, one for each chromatic note") fails because it confuses diatonic with chromatic.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: How much motion a tritone resolution uses

stimulus.body: A short reference note on how much motion a tritone resolution uses is set for a close-reading task. It states: Semitone proximity means minimal motion. A marginal reminder adds: smallest possible distance. Four statements are then offered, and only one of them follows from what the note actually says.

questions.stem: The excerpt is probed with “Describe tritone motion / Smallest possible distance. / How much motion a tritone resolution uses”. Which choice is defensible?

answer.exemplar: Each tendency tone lies one semitone from its target, so the resolution moves the smallest possible distance, making it both efficient and strongly directed.

questions.explanation: The passage gives the controlling distinction: semitone proximity means minimal motion. On that basis "Each tendency tone lies one semitone from its target, so the resolution moves the smallest…" is the supported choice.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Why the dominant to tonic progression is the strongest

stimulus.body: Read this source excerpt carefully: «The strength comes from the dominant's tendency tones resolving to tonic's stable tones, releasing tension and creating a clear sense of arrival.» Tendency tones resolve to stable tonic tones. A marginal reminder adds: tension release to rest. It is followed by four candidate interpretations, of which exactly one is supported by the wording of the excerpt.

questions.stem: A student recalls “Explain strength source / Tension release to rest. / Why the dominant to tonic progression is the strongest” before answering. Which choice should they make?

answer.exemplar: The strength comes from the dominant's tendency tones resolving to tonic's stable tones, releasing tension and creating a clear sense of arrival.

questions.explanation: Close reading of the note yields this rule: tendency tones resolve to stable tonic tones. On that basis "The strength comes from the dominant's tendency tones resolving to tonic's stable tones,…" is the supported choice.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: The distance from a triad's third to its fifth

stimulus.body: The working note below records the evidence for a claim about the distance from a triad's third to its fifth. the upper interval of a major triad is a minor third. A marginal reminder adds: upper interval is minor third. A reader must decide which of the four proposed statements the note warrants, without using outside knowledge.

questions.stem: The check to perform is “State upper interval of triad / Upper interval is minor third. / The distance from a triad's third to its fifth”. Which option passes that check?

options.text: A tritone, confusing triad with seventh chord
A major third, confusing with the root-to-third interval
A perfect fourth, overcounting the span
options.misconception: selects "A perfect fourth, overcounting the span" where the rule in the passage requires a different condition

options.text: A minor third, because the fifth is perfect

questions.explanation: What settles the item is the relation stated in the passage: the upper interval of a major triad is a minor third. On that basis "A minor third, because the fifth is perfect" is the supported choice. Option A ("A tritone, confusing triad with seventh chord") fails because it confuses chord types; Option B ("A major third, confusing with the root-to-third interval") fails because it confuses intervals; Option C ("A perfect fourth, overcounting the span") fails because it selects "A perfect fourth, overcounting the span" where the distance from a triad's third to its fifth requires a different condition.
